t.2.24.1: Addressed in this way, Vaidehī, who deserved only kindness and always spoke kindly, grew angry out of sheer love and said this to her husband.
t.2.24.2: O noble lord, a father, a mother, a brother, a son, and likewise a daughter-in-law each enjoy the fruits of their own merits and abide by their own allotted fortune.
t.2.24.3: A wife alone shares in her husband's fortune, O bull among men; therefore I too have been commanded that I must dwell in the forest.
t.2.24.4: Neither father nor son, nor one's own self, nor mother, nor the company of friends, but the husband alone is ever the refuge of women, both here and after death.
t.2.24.5: If you have set out this very day for the impassable forest, O Rāghava, I shall walk ahead of you, trampling down the kuśa grass and thorns.
t.2.24.6: Casting aside jealousy and anger like water left over after drinking, take me with you, O hero, without misgiving; there is no wrong in me.
t.2.24.7: The shade of a husband's feet, whatever one's circumstances, is better than the summits of palaces, than celestial chariots, or even than travelling through the sky.
t.2.24.9: I shall dwell happily in the forest, just as in my father's house, giving no thought to the three worlds and thinking only of my vow of devotion to my husband.
t.2.24.8: I have been instructed by my mother and by my father in matters of every kind; I need not be told now how I ought to conduct myself.
t.2.24.10: Ever serving you, self-restrained and living in chastity, I shall delight with you, O hero, in the forests fragrant with honey.
t.2.24.11: For you, O Rāma, are able to provide full protection in the forest even to any other person here; how much more then to me, O giver of honour?
t.2.24.12: I shall always live on fruits and roots, there is no doubt of it. Dwelling with you, I shall cause you no sorrow.
t.2.24.13: I wish to see rivers, mountains, ponds and forests everywhere, free from fear, with you, my wise lord, as my protector.
t.2.24.14: Happy in the company of you, my hero, I would wish to behold lotus ponds in full and lovely bloom, thronged with haṃsa geese and kāraṇḍava ducks.
t.2.24.15: With you, O large-eyed one, I shall take my delight, supremely joyful; and thus I would be with you even for a hundred thousand years.
t.2.24.16: O Rāghava, tiger among men, if my dwelling even in heaven were to be without you, I would not find even that pleasing.
t.2.24.17: I shall go to the forest, so very hard to traverse, teeming with deer and filled with monkeys and elephants. Clasping your feet alone and cherished by you, I shall dwell in the forest as in my father's house.
t.2.24.18: Take me with you, for I think of no one else, my heart is devoted to you, and parted from you I am resolved to die. Kindly grant my request; because of me no burden will fall upon you from this.
t.2.24.19: Even though she spoke thus, the best of men, devoted to dharma, did not wish to take Sītā with him, and he spoke at length to her in her distress, urging her to turn back and telling her about life in the forest.
